title: A War of 1812 soldier buried his own arm. His real story is even stranger
originalTitle: A War of 1812 soldier buried his own arm. His real story is even stranger
content:
Archival discoveries, including a long-forgotten 19th-century autobiography, are changing how historians understand Shadrack Byfield, an English veteran of the War of 1812 who buried his own amputated arm and later created a custom prosthesis.

Byfield has appeared repeatedly in television documentaries, books, and museum exhibits in the USA and Canada, where he has often been portrayed as a stoic British soldier who endured hardship without complaint. Newly uncovered evidence presents a much more complicated picture. It shows a determined veteran who spent years demanding better benefits while struggling with chronic pain, poverty, employers, and the police.

'They came and pushed me about, and spat in my face, hoping that I should strike them, in order if possible, to take away my pension … They reported that I intended to shoot two of the deacons.'

Those words come from Byfield himself, describing an encounter at his local chapel in Gloucestershire during the 1850s, when he was 63 and living with the effects of his wartime injuries. By then, he had become caught up in a fierce dispute among village Baptists. He would later be accused of cutting an opponent across the face with the iron crook attached to his wooden arm.

A Lost Memoir Reveals Years of Pain

Elsewhere in his rediscovered autobiography, Byfield described how injuries from the war continued to affect him decades after the fighting ended:

'It now pleased the Lord to afflict me with a violent rheumatic pain in my right shoulder, from which the [musket] ball was cut out. I was in this condition for nearly three years: -- oftentimes I was not able to lift my hand to my head, nor a tea-cup to my mouth'.

He was equally outspoken when he believed his disability was being used as a reason to pay him less. After an employer refused to give him full wages for working as a one-handed gardener, Byfield declared: 'I never saw the man that would compete with me with one arm'.

While a Cambridge University historian, Dr. Eamonn O'Keeffe discovered what he believes is the only surviving copy of Byfield's History and Conversion of a British Soldier. Published in London, England, in 1851, the autobiography resurfaced roughly 3,700 miles away in the library of the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland, Ohio. O'Keeffe published his findings in the Journal of British Studies (Cambridge University Press).

"Byfield's account of his wartime experiences is quite well known but the man behind the memoir has remained elusive. Uncovering these new details about his life provides remarkable insight into the suffering and resilience of Britain's homecoming soldiers," says Dr. O'Keeffe.

A Familiar Soldier With an Unknown Life

The War of 1812 was fought in North America between the United States and the United Kingdom as the Napoleonic Wars were drawing toward an end in Europe. The conflict became an important episode in the formation of national identity in both the US and Canada.

Historians have long valued Byfield's first memoir because it provides the unusual perspective of an ordinary British soldier fighting around the Great Lakes. His experiences have appeared in history books and documentaries, including PBS's 'The War of 1812' (2011). He was also the central character in Gregory Sass's 1985 children's novel Redcoat, and the Fort Erie Visitor Centre in Ontario has a display dedicated to him.

For years, researchers believed Byfield had died around 1850. The discovery of his 1851 memoir, combined with evidence O'Keeffe located in newspapers and other archival records, shows that his story continued for more than two decades beyond that assumed date.

From Wiltshire to War in Canada

Byfield was born near the Wiltshire textile town of Bradford-on-Avon in 1789. At age eighteen, he joined the Wiltshire militia in 1807. According to Byfield, the decision devastated his mother so deeply that she fell into a speechless fit and died only days later.

He soon volunteered to join the regular army and sailed for Canada in 1809, where he entered the 41st Regiment of Foot. When the United States declared war in June 1812, Byfield was stationed at Fort George on the Niagara River.

He went on to participate in several significant battles and survived a wound to the neck. Then, in 1814, a musket ball smashed his left forearm.

The injury required the lower part of his arm to be sawn off without anesthetic. A medical orderly then tossed the severed limb onto a 'dung-heap'. Furious, Byfield retrieved his arm and insisted on burying it properly. He nailed several boards together to create a makeshift coffin for the limb.

A year later, he traveled to the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London to be assessed for an army pension. The decision left him 'very much dissatisfied' because he was awarded only nine pence per day.

An Inventive Prosthesis and a Fight for Work

After returning to Bradford-on-Avon, Byfield initially supported himself as a farm laborer. His missing forearm prevented him from immediately returning to his previous occupation as a weaver.

According to his later account, the solution came to him in a dream. Byfield envisioned an "instrument" that could allow him to work a loom despite his disability. He then asked a local blacksmith to turn his idea into a functional device.

The prosthesis helped him return to weaving, but that was not his only source of income. He also worked as a 'chairman' in nearby Bath, transporting sick and infirm people through the city's steep streets in wheelchairs and sedan chairs despite his own physical injuries.

At the same time, Byfield began a determined effort to have his pension increased. He eventually succeeded in 1836 with the assistance of Sir William Napier, a retired army officer and prominent military historian.

In 1840, Byfield published his first book-length autobiography, A Narrative of a Light Company Soldier's Service. He has commonly been described as illiterate, but O'Keeffe uncovered a draft of the memoir among Napier's papers that was written in Byfield's own hand.

Two Memoirs Tell Two Different Stories

The image Byfield presented in his 1840 memoir differs sharply from the one found in his later autobiography.

"In the 1840 narrative, Byfield sought to impress wealthy patrons by presenting himself as a dutiful soldier and deserving veteran," O'Keeffe says. "The 1851 memoir, by contrast, was a spiritual redemption story, with Byfield tracing his progress from rebellious sinner to devout and repentant Christian."

The later memoir also contains admissions that make Byfield appear less conventionally heroic. He acknowledged leaving camp without permission and taking part in a plundering expedition with other soldiers.

"Such unflattering incidents are conspicuously absent from Byfield's earlier accounts of his military service," O'Keeffe says. "In the 1851 memoir, the veteran also dwells on periods of indebtedness, illness and unemployment after returning to England, whereas in his earlier memoir he described maintaining his family 'comfortably' with his weaving prosthesis for nearly twenty years."

His recollections also reveal how physically demanding it was to resume work after losing an arm. Byfield wrote that when an employer required him to operate his loom with one hand:

'I endeavored … as well as I could, but I found my arm very much fatigued. I scarcely knew what to do. I went into my bed-chamber, knelt before the Lord, and begged of Him to give me strength to labor … To the honor and praise of His dear name, that arm has been enabled to perform the work as well as the other.'

A Bitter Feud Ends in a Chapel Riot

Later in life, Byfield moved to Hawkesbury Upton in Gloucestershire. There, he became deeply involved in a struggle over control of the village's Particular Baptist chapel.

The dispute escalated far beyond theological disagreement. It involved lawsuits, physical fights, arson, and vandalism before reaching a dramatic peak with a riot inside the chapel in June 1853.

O'Keeffe reconstructed the episode by comparing Byfield's 1851 memoir with contemporary newspaper reports and legal records.

Byfield was accused of starting the confrontation "by pushing about" and then cutting an adversary around the eye and face with the iron hook on his prosthetic arm.

The following day, police sergeant Sidney Short served him with a summons. Short had previously tried, unsuccessfully, to prosecute Byfield for public drunkenness two years earlier.

According to Short, Byfield, the chapel's minister, and another man responded with 'torrents of abuse'. He said the men spat at him and chased him into the street. Byfield, meanwhile, accused the policeman of giving false testimony during the earlier drunkenness case.

The Cost of the Chapel Conflict

Byfield was never convicted of assault, but the dispute still had serious consequences. His faction eventually lost control of the chapel.

He also lost his job as keeper of a 100-foot monument dedicated to Lord Edward Somerset, a general who fought at Waterloo. Eighteen parishioners successfully petitioned the Duke of Beaufort to remove Byfield from the position.

The job had been especially valuable because it included the use of a cottage. Byfield had originally obtained the post after selling a copy of his military memoir to the duke while employed as a tollkeeper.

In 1856, Byfield moved back to Bradford-on-Avon and married his second wife. Sir William Napier continued providing him with an annual allowance, and Byfield traveled to London when his longtime patron died in 1860.

He kept seeking further increases to his military pension, but those later requests were unsuccessful.

By 1867, Byfield was selling another memoir titled The Forlorn Hope. No surviving copies are currently known.

He died in January 1874 at the age of 84.

A More Complicated Picture of Disabled Veterans

The rediscovered evidence challenges the simplified image of Byfield as a soldier who quietly accepted his circumstances. Instead, it reveals a man who repeatedly pushed back when he believed he was being treated unfairly, even as he endured lasting physical pain, financial hardship, and emotional strain.

"Byfield's 1851 memoir emphasizes the challenges of post-war reintegration, especially for veterans with disabilities, in the decades after the Napoleonic Wars. It also demonstrates ex-soldiers' determination to secure the support they felt they were owed," O'Keeffe says. "My work also busts the myth that Byfield always did what he was told and never complained. He was very strong-willed but also suffered a great deal of hardship and psychological strain."

Eamonn O'Keeffe is the Ewart A. Pratt Fellow in Military, Naval, and Maritime History at Memorial University in Newfoundland, Canada. From 2022 to September 2025, he was a National Army Museum Fellow at Queens' College, Cambridge.
